question: Why does the mathematician Jordan Ellenberg warn that not every curve is a straight line?
answer: Because many relationships rise, then fall. His example is the Laffer curve: a tax rate of zero raises no money, and nor does a rate of 100 percent, so revenue peaks somewhere between. Whether raising a tax raises revenue depends on where you are on the curve, so both sides can have a point.
move: More of a good thing isn't always better; look for the peak.
simply: A tax of zero raises nothing, and a tax of 100 percent raises nothing too, since nobody bothers working. The best rate lies somewhere in between.
why: Exercise, sleep, spending and medicine often work the same way: some helps, too much harms. Asking where the peak is beats arguing more versus less.
source: Jordan Ellenberg, How Not to Be Wrong, 2014
reference: Jordan Ellenberg, How Not to Be Wrong: The Power of Mathematical Thinking (Penguin Press, 2014), ch. 1
